# Cambridge Ms. Add. 1753 Page Images

`cam1753/cam1753-spreads/` held fourteen two-page spreads, archive pages 0077 through 0090,
until 2026-09-26, when
[`../doc/PLAN-retire-codex-index-image-work.md`](../doc/PLAN-retire-codex-index-image-work.md)
removed them with the programs that read them. The last commit that holds them is
`1fba91fed6f22cd5aeb4d56d836cf109de48b8ad`, so Git history restores the exact files:
`git show 1fba91fe:cam1753/cam1753-spreads/cam1753-page-0077.jpg`, for example, gives the
first spread. The Internet Archive item below can supply a fresh copy. The 28 single
pages split from the spreads were never tracked: they lived in the ignored
`cam1753-pages/`, which was retired with the spreads.

## Source

Downloaded from the Internet Archive, by `py/main_cam1753_download_spreads.py`, which was
retired with the spreads; `git show 1fba91fe:py/py_cam1753_loc/download_spreads.py`
recovers the module it ran:

<https://archive.org/details/ketuvim-cambridge-ms-add-1753-images>

## Page-split naming convention

The archive.org images are two-page spreads (the codex photographed while
open). Each spread shows the verso (B side) of one leaf on the right and
the recto (A side) of the next leaf on the left — as if the codex is
actually spread open.

The split files in `cam1753-pages/` were named `{leaf:04d}{side}.jpg`
where side is `A` (recto) or `B` (verso). The leaf number is derived from
the numbering visible on the left page of each spread:

- The left page of archive page N bears leaf number N − 4.
- The right page is the verso of the preceding leaf, i.e. leaf N − 5.

For example, archive page 0077 yields `0072B.jpg` (right) and `0073A.jpg`
(left).

The leaf numbers on the manuscript pages appear both in Western Arabic
numerals written in pencil (e.g. "73") and in Hebrew numerals
(e.g. "עג").

## Alternate image set

There appears to be an alternate set of digital images for Cambridge
Ms. Add. 1753 on the Internet Archive:

<https://archive.org/details/20230306_20230306_1051/mode/1up>

It is not yet known how these images differ from the ones
we use — e.g. whether they are overall better, worse, or neutral in
quality.
